## Constraints Push Back {#sec-lay-ch06}

## A Concrete Picture

A key on a taut cord cannot follow an arbitrary path relative to your hand.
The cord pulls along its length and changes the key's acceleration. It cannot
push: if the motion would require compression, the cord goes slack and the taut
constraint stops applying. Cut it without an impulse and the key retains its
instantaneous velocity, tangent to the former circle for a stationary hand.
Gravity then bends its subsequent trajectory. The tangent is an initial
direction, not a promise of straight-line flight.

A rigid pin can transmit forces in either direction; a cord cannot. A shoe can
push against the ground but normally cannot pull the ground upward, and its
resistance to slipping is limited by contact conditions. These distinctions
matter before solving any equations. A mathematically enforceable motion need
not be physically feasible for the chosen connection.

The shared lesson is useful in the golf swing: **zero selected motor torque does
not imply zero connection force**. A wrist can transmit force while its modeled
torque command is zero. Two separated hand forces can oppose one another yet
produce a club moment. The ground reaction depends on the complete constrained
motion, not on a single local command. None of those observations identifies
which human muscles are active.

![An Ideal Circular Guide Changes Acceleration; the Tangent Marks Release Velocity, Not a Gravity-Affected Future Trajectory.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_constraint_reaction.svg){#fig-lay-constraint-reaction width=78% fig-pos="H" fig-alt="A schematic circular guide with an inward reaction and a perpendicular instantaneous velocity. The dotted tangent indicates the velocity direction at release; a cord can supply the inward force only while its tension is nonnegative."}

## How the Mechanism Works

### Geometry and Dynamics Must Agree

For a smooth, time-independent holonomic constraint, write
$\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf q)=0$. Here $\mathbf q$ contains configuration
coordinates, $\mathbf J=\partial\boldsymbol\phi/\partial\mathbf q$ maps their
rates into constraint rates, and dots mean time derivatives along the motion.
The compatible velocity and acceleration satisfy
$\mathbf J\dot{\mathbf q}=0$ and
$\mathbf J\ddot{\mathbf q}+\dot{\mathbf J}\dot{\mathbf q}=0$.
The second term is essential: a key moving around a circle has inward
acceleration even at constant speed.

For the coordinate convention in which generalized velocity is
$\dot{\mathbf q}$, one common simultaneous solve is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf M & -\mathbf J^{\mathsf T}\\
\mathbf J & \mathbf 0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\ddot{\mathbf q}\\
\boldsymbol\lambda
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf Q-\mathbf h\\
-\dot{\mathbf J}\dot{\mathbf q}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$\mathbf M$ is the inertia matrix; $\mathbf Q$ contains declared applied
generalized loads, including controls; $\mathbf h$ contains the remaining
bias terms under the chosen gravity convention. The generalized constraint
load is $\mathbf Q_c=\mathbf J^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\lambda$.
A multiplier is not automatically a Cartesian force in newtons: its meaning
and units depend on how the constraint equation is defined and scaled.
In formulations using generalized speeds $\mathbf v$ with
$\dot{\mathbf q}=\mathbf N(\mathbf q)\mathbf v$, the corresponding velocity
Jacobian and dynamics must be used consistently. Here $\mathbf N$ maps
generalized speeds into coordinate rates.

Positive-definite $\mathbf M$ and independent rows of $\mathbf J$ make this
fixed-state bilateral system nonsingular. It requires compatible initial
position and velocity. Integrating only the acceleration equation can still
accumulate position or velocity drift; numerical projection or stabilization
must be audited separately from physical forces and work. These distinctions
follow the [multibody formulation](https://underactuated.mit.edu/multibody.html)
and are developed further in the book's forward-model discussion.

The solve is valid within its declared contact mode. A solution demanding
negative cord tension, tensile ground contact, or excessive sticking friction
cannot be rescued by calling its multiplier a reaction. The mode or model must
change. Impacts additionally require an impulse/contact treatment; this smooth
acceleration equation is not an impact law.

### A Circle Checks the Signs

At the top of a one-metre circle, a two-kilogram key has required vertical
acceleration $-v^2/(1\,\mathrm m)$, with upward positive. Use terrestrial
gravity $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and let $\lambda$ denote the guide's
upward reaction in newtons. Newton's law gives
$\lambda=mg-mv^2/(1\,\mathrm m)$.
At $v=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the required reaction is $+17.62\,\mathrm N$:
an enclosing bilateral guide could push upward, but a cord from the centre
could not. At $v=4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, it is $-12.38\,\mathrm N$, so
the required inward tension is feasible in this idealized example.

This is a manufactured sign-and-feasibility check, not a golfer parameter
estimate. It shows why solving an equality and checking the permitted force
direction are distinct operations.

### Zero Virtual Work Is Not Always Zero Actual Work

An ideal constraint is defined through virtual work: its generalized load
pairs to zero with every allowed virtual displacement at a fixed instant.
That is a force--displacement pairing, not necessarily Euclidean
perpendicularity in a mixed set of angular and translational coordinates.
For stationary ideal constraints, the actual compatible velocity is also in
the allowed tangent space, giving zero total constraint power.

A prescribed moving support changes the result. If
$\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf q,t)=0$, then
$\mathbf J\dot{\mathbf q}+\boldsymbol\phi_t=0$, and therefore

$$
P_c=\mathbf Q_c^{\mathsf T}\dot{\mathbf q}
=\boldsymbol\lambda^{\mathsf T}\mathbf J\dot{\mathbf q}
=-\boldsymbol\lambda^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\phi_t.
$$

This can be nonzero even for an ideal constraint. The support's drive supplies
or absorbs that power. Here $\boldsymbol\phi_t$ is the partial time derivative
at fixed configuration. The acceleration condition must also retain the full
time derivative of the moving-constraint velocity condition; the autonomous
formula above cannot simply be reused with its explicit-time terms omitted.

An existing manufactured example makes the accounting concrete. A two-kilogram
mass follows the prescribed guide $x(t)=\alpha t^2$, with
$\alpha=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. At one second, $v=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
and $a=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. A separate applied force of $3\,\mathrm N$
leaves a $1\,\mathrm N$ guide reaction. Their powers are $6\,\mathrm W$
and $2\,\mathrm W$, summing to the $8\,\mathrm W$ kinetic-energy rate.
The moving guide's work must appear in the selected system's ledger.

This is the same boundary issue encountered with a prescribed torso or hand
path. If the support is outside the model, its reaction power is external.
If its driven body is included, account for that body's actuator, storage,
and other interactions instead of treating the imposed motion as free energy.

### Zero Total Constraint Power Can Hide Transfer Between Bodies

Now consider a passive ideal pin joining two bodies. At their common point,
compatible velocities and equal-and-opposite connection forces give opposite
one-sided powers. The sum is zero, but either body's contribution can be large.
A powered wagon can pull an unpowered wagon through such a connection, raising
the latter's kinetic energy without a motor on it.

For a connection that also transmits a couple, include the moment--angular-
velocity pairing. Total cancellation requires the corresponding compatible
relative motion; force cancellation by itself is insufficient. Slip,
deformation, interface inertia, or actuation changes the ledger. An ideal
rigid constraint has no elastic storage state. A compliant element replacing
it may store strain energy, while damping dissipates energy.

This explains how a wrist reaction can contribute to club power without
creating energy for the complete chain. A rigid foot held stationary against
rigid ground has zero contact-wrench power because its contact twist vanishes,
while the support still enables internal actuators to accelerate the golfer
and club. The contact conditions and system boundary must be stated before
either claim is applied.

### Three Different Questions About Reaction Uniqueness

**A forward model with known inputs.** Given its complete state, applied loads,
inertia, and independent bilateral constraints, the nonsingular system above
determines acceleration and multipliers uniquely. Having two hands or a closed
loop does not, by itself, make that solve indeterminate. The pinned provider's
planar two-hand model has seven coordinates and four independent scalar
point-coincidence constraints; it rejects rank loss rather than silently
choosing a different allocation.

**A redundant description.** If rows of $\mathbf J$ repeat the same restriction,
different multipliers can produce the same generalized load. For example, with
rows $(1,0)$ and $(2,0)$, multipliers $(-2,0)$ and $(-0.4,-0.8)$ both give
$\mathbf J^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\lambda=(-2,0)$.
The latter has smaller Euclidean multiplier norm. Rescaling the second
equation changes the minimum-norm numbers again without changing the physical
restriction. For positive-definite inertia and compatible redundant
acceleration equations, acceleration can remain unique while multipliers are
not. Inconsistent equations instead have no exact solution. A pseudoinverse
does not turn an inconsistent residual into physical evidence.

**Inference from incomplete observations.** Measuring the club's resultant
wrench is a different problem. It supplies fewer conditions than a detailed
description of two hand-contact wrenches, and the required biological inputs
are usually unknown. A complete model can provide additional equations or
constitutive assumptions; sensors can provide additional observations.
Identifiability then depends on what those additions actually determine.
Neither a solver's preferred allocation nor a club trajectory alone measures
muscle recruitment. Chapter 25 follows this inference problem inward from
hand loads to joint demand and musculotendon forces.

### Opposing Forces Do Not Necessarily Cancel the Wrench

Let hand-force increments be $+\mathbf f$ and $-\mathbf f$ at fixed club
points $\mathbf r_L$ and $\mathbf r_R$. Their net-force change is zero, but
their moment change about the same origin is

$$
\Delta\mathbf M=(\mathbf r_L-\mathbf r_R)\times\mathbf f.
$$

For points $0.2\,\mathrm m$ apart along the club's local $x$ axis, opposite
$1\,\mathrm N$ transverse forces produce a $0.2\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ couple.
Opposite axial increments along the separation vector instead give zero
complete-wrench change. Contact couples, if permitted, must also be included when testing a
wrench-neutral allocation.

Such an algebraic load change need not be feasible under friction, strength,
joint, or constitutive constraints. Nor does zero resultant wrench guarantee
zero deformation or identical tissue demand. It leaves the rigid club's
instantaneous Newton--Euler load unchanged under the stated geometry and other
loads; it does not by itself establish stability or a beneficial squeeze.
Two-foot load inference has analogous limits. Separate six-axis force plates
can add bilateral wrench information. Ordinary pressure-only insoles measure
normal pressure; their shear and full-wrench estimates require additional
information or modeling.

### Radial Force, Moment, and Power Ask Different Questions

For a straight rigid club, a wrist force directed along the line from wrist to
club centre of mass has zero moment about that centre. A transverse component
has a lever arm and contributes to the rotational balance. The complete
acceleration still depends on translation, other loads, any applied couple,
and the connected bodies. A component's name does not isolate a causal driver.

Force power uses the force's application-point velocity. A force radial to
the club can therefore perform hand-point work when that point moves along it.
By contrast, the proximal centripetal term in the provider's fixed-hub planar
decomposition is radial to the *arm* and perpendicular to the wrist velocity,
so that particular term has zero wrist-force power. Those two uses of
"radial" are not interchangeable. The signed dot product resolves the issue.

### Remove an Input Without Counting the Drift Twice

A pointwise counterfactual copies the full state and time, removes specified
commands, and solves again with the other declared loads and constraints
retained. The resulting zero-command reaction is not a force-free wrist, a
measurement of passive tissue, or a statement about human effort.

For a fixed smooth contact mode and dynamics affine in two declared inputs
(proximal $P$ and distal $D$),
let $\mathbf y_{PD}$ denote the response with both inputs, $\mathbf y_P$ and
$\mathbf y_D$ the respective single-input cases, and $\mathbf y_0$ the
zero-input case. The response can include acceleration and reactions. Then

$$
\mathbf y_{PD}
=\mathbf y_0+(\mathbf y_P-\mathbf y_0)+(\mathbf y_D-\mathbf y_0)
=\mathbf y_P+\mathbf y_D-\mathbf y_0.
$$

Simply adding the two single-input runs counts shared gravity, velocity,
external-load, and constraint-bias effects twice. For endpoint position
$\mathbf x(\mathbf q)$, the kinematic Jacobian
$\mathbf J_x=\partial\mathbf x/\partial\mathbf q$ gives
$\mathbf a_x=\mathbf J_x\ddot{\mathbf q}+\dot{\mathbf J}_x\dot{\mathbf q}$.
That changing-Jacobian contribution belongs in the fixed-state baseline too.
The identity does not generally survive a contact-mode
change, a nonlinear input map, or comparison of different states.

A forward killswitch begins from the same state but removes a command over an
interval. The trajectories then diverge, and later differences include that
changed history. Retaining an open-loop command history is different from
retaining a feedback policy whose outputs change with the state. Report the
chosen continuation.

### Compliance Is a Model With Its Own Dynamics

A force--extension law stores strain energy; a static stiffness value is not a
time delay. Inertia, damping, relaxation, activation, and wave propagation can
introduce timescales in a more complete model. Specify which mechanism is
present instead of attributing all timing to compliance.

Making a penalty spring stiffer also creates faster dynamics. For a
one-kilogram undamped mass with initial extension $F_0/k$ and zero velocity,
where $F_0=1\,\mathrm N$, the extension is
$\delta(t)=(F_0/k)\cos(\sqrt{k/m}\,t)$.
Its amplitude and initial stored energy $F_0^2/(2k)$ tend to zero as $k$
increases, yet the spring-force amplitude remains $1\,\mathrm N$.
Vanishing displacement alone therefore does not establish uniform convergence
of reaction forces to the rigid model.

A useful rigid/compliant comparison declares initial compatibility, damping,
contact law, integration accuracy, and the observable whose convergence is
claimed. Resolve the fast modes or justify a reduced description. Track
constraint residuals and numerical energy changes alongside the physical
work ledger. Successful convergence of one observable is not human validation
of the chosen compliance.

### What the Evidence Establishes

**Model Result:** The pinned double-pendulum source derives nonzero wrist
reactions after specified torque removal and separates force magnitude from
signed wrist-force power. Its forward two-hand extension reports a finite
negative-couple persistence interval after all six applied commands are cut.
Those are declared model results, not new simulations performed for this
chapter, universal persistence, or measurements of biological passivity.

**Human Evidence:** Koike's 2016 instrumented-grip report describes a
professional instructor and a design with twelve sets of strain gauges
[@koike2016instrumented]. Choi and Park's
2020 study used a six-axis sensor between sections of a customized grip in
nine right-handed male professional golfers, combined with motion capture and
inverse dynamics [@koike2020]. The internal sensor
wrench is measured; the remaining joint loads are inferred through the model.
The latter study reports limitations including altered instrument mass,
hand-contact coupling, foam-ball impact, and rigid-segment assumptions.
Its measurements improve load inference without identifying individual muscle
forces or establishing an optimal intervention.

**Hypothesis:** An achieved late-downswing state may permit favorable club
acceleration or power through connection forces while selected distal commands
are small or opposing. Specify the observable, sign, interval, load limits,
and alternative models before testing it. Large reactions or a negative
couple alone do not establish that hypothesis.

### Reader Lab and Ways the Claim Could Fail

Run all-input, proximal-only, distal-only, and zero-input cases from one copied
state. Compare the reactions and endpoint accelerations using the shared-drift
identity above. Check the physical force directions and contact limits before
accepting a branch. Then integrate explicitly defined continuations and compare
power, work, delivery events, and trajectory divergence.

Change geometry through constraint-consistent states. A force component's
projection may reverse under a specified geometric transformation, but the
recomputed reaction can also change; an arbitrary angle reversal need not
reverse total transfer. Changing coordinate signs consistently must leave
physical predictions unchanged. Removing a force lever arm has a sharper null
prediction: its moment contribution vanishes, while separately applied couples
must remain separately accounted for.

A claimed mechanism is undermined by failure of its registered counterfactual
effect, force/moment balance, work ledger, admissible contact conditions, or
observable convergence. Agreement between independent solvers strengthens the
numerical result only to the extent their methods and assumptions are actually
independent. Human relevance additionally needs synchronized load and motion
measurements, uncertainty, participant-held-out predictions, and evidence that
the model represents the tested task.

### One Sentence to Retain

A connection can transmit force and transfer energy between bodies without
being an independent energy source; its physical feasibility, power, and
inferred biological meaning are three separate questions.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The circular guide is a deliberately simple example. A human wrist has multiple
degrees of freedom, deformable tissues, muscle action, and distributed contact;
the shoulder girdle and grip can move. Ideal point constraints omit those
features. Their multipliers cannot be read directly as tissue stresses,
muscle forces, injury estimates, or coaching instructions.

Keep three boundaries visible: the permitted motion and contact mode; the
complete system whose energy is counted; and the measurements or assumptions
used to identify loads. A plausible mechanism can survive those checks and
remain an untested hypothesis about how a particular golfer produces it.
